title: From Sterilization to New Life: Vasectomy, Regret, and Reversal
author: Grant Martsolf
summary: Grant Martsolf, a health policy researcher, tells the story of his vasectomy at 34, his and his wife's regret within six months, and the reversal that eventually led to a new baby. He explains that the decision was driven by exhaustion, financial stress and a community where vasectomies had become normalized and even joked about, and that the procedure was fully covered by insurance. He then marshals data: about 500,000 US men get a vasectomy each year, roughly 18 percent by age 45, and nearly 20 percent later want more children, yet only about 6 percent actually reverse it. Cost is a major barrier, since reversals are rarely covered. His own reversal in 2021 was followed three years later by a pregnancy, but he still grieves the children who might have been born in the intervening decade. He concludes that couples in a vulnerable moment would benefit from more friction nudging them toward openness to life.
points: Martsolf presents regret after vasectomy as common rather than rare, citing nearly 20 percent of men who want more children afterward.
Social normalization and full insurance coverage made the procedure frictionless, while reversal costs about $15,000 and is mostly uncovered.
Their regret was spiritual as well as practical and contributed to their conversion to the Catholic Church.
Only about 6 percent of vasectomized men reverse the procedure, and remarriage is the strongest predictor, showing how rarely second thoughts become action.
He argues the asymmetry in cost and ease should be weighed, since a small barrier at the time of decision might have changed his family.
quotes: Within the first six months of having the procedure, my wife and I were overcome with the sense that we had done something gravely wrong.
About 500,000 men get a vasectomy each year in the United States. By the age of 45, about 18% of American men will have had one.

In fact, regret is not unusual when it comes to vasectomies. Vasectomy supporters say “most men are satisfied with their vasectomy”—true enough. Yet nearly 20% of men who have had the procedure desire more children after their vasectomy.

Despite the relative ease of the procedure and the success rates, very few men end up having a reversal. Roughly 10% of those who have had a vasectomy return for a consultation to explore surgical options, and around 6% will ultimately have the reversal.
In contrast to the vasectomy procedure, which is considered medically necessary by most providers, there is almost no insurance coverage for vasectomy reversals.
During the ride home from the procedure with my family, the realization of what I had done really hit me: our family was open to life once more!

I realize that my wife and I made the decision to have the vasectomy on our own, but I also wish that in that time of great vulnerability, there had been a bit more resistance—nudging us toward openness to life.
